## Our goal

The central question of the Multimodal Cognitive Neuroscience Lab is how people use visual information to navigate the complex social world. Specifically, we aim to understand the neural computations and network-level dynamics that transform detailed visual representations of faces and objects into meaningful representations of identity, social evaluation, and memory. We are also interested in examining how this process distorted in individuals with neuropsychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia and autism.

## Complementary modalities

We use a multimodal neuroscience platform, capable of capturing neural signals across multiple spatial scales, spanning microscopic (single neuron and local field potential) to mesoscopic (iEEG and 7T fMRI), and to macroscopic (3T fMRI) levels. These signals are combined with computational modeling, eye tracking, and behavioral measurement to delineate neurocomputational and circuit-level mechanisms across multiple spatial scales underlying human cognition.

### Functional MRI

Ultra-high-field fMRI maps fine-grained BOLD responses and distributed representations across the human brain.

## Research themes

::: {.research-grid}
::: {.research-card}
### Face and object perception

How does the brain transform detailed visual information into stable representations of identities, concepts, and social attributes? We study this transformation across a distributed network spanning ventral temporal, medial temporal, and prefrontal areas by surveying the distribution of coding schemes and interareal interactions. 
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Social inferences

Beyond recognizing identities, we spontaneously observe people’s emotional states and form first impressions from faces. These inferences are context-dependent and influenced by factors such as task demands and prior experience. How the underlying neural computations and functional connectivity change across different task contexts, such as emotion and social trait inferences? How face representations evolve dynamically under naturalistic viewing conditions? To address these questions, we will: 1) quantify and compare neural face models across multiple task contexts, including free viewing, emotion recognition, and social trait judgment; 2) examine dynamic neural computations using naturalistic video stimuli; 3) investigate context-dependent reconfiguration of functional networks. 
:::


::: {.research-card}
### Neuropyschiatric disorders

Social deficits are hallmark features of various neurodevelopment and psychiatric disorders, including autism and SCZ, both of which have been broadly associated with atypical face processing. However, the neural computational mechanisms underlying these impairments remain largely unclear. We aim to test how computational frameworks of face and object established in neurotypical populations distort in these clinical conditions and associate with social dysfunction. 
:::

::: {.research-card}
### Multimodal integration

Single-neuron recordings, iEEG, and fMRI reveal different aspects of the same neural system across space and time. We are developing quantitative approaches that align these scales into coherent mechanistic accounts of how visual information becomes meaningful. We aim to determine whether measurements made at different scales support the same computational explanation, from the selectivity of individual neurons, through the timing and coordination of local and distributed neural populations, to the fine-grained and whole-brain organization measured with fMRI. 
:::


## Collaborative environment

Our home in the [Neuroimaging Labs Research Center](https://www.mir.wustl.edu/research/research-centers/neuroimaging-labs-research-center-nil-rc/) provides a highly collaborative environment spanning human cognitive and clinical neuroscience, systems neuroscience, neurodevelopment, advanced imaging, and quantitative analysis. We welcome collaborations that bring together complementary scientific questions, datasets, and methods.
